* Appeal from the following judgment to the Supreme Court of Canada (Lamer C.J. and La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory, McLachlin and Major JJ.) dismissed March 24, 1994.  S.C.C. File No. 23023, 23097.  S.C.C. Bulletin, 1994, p. 598.  Full text of the SCC judgment is available at
1994 CanLII 129 (SCC)
, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 701 in the SCJ database.
Criminal law -- Practice, process and procedure -- Intervention -- Canadian Holocaust Remembrance Association denied leave to intervene in Crown appeal against acquittal of person charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The moving party, a non-profit organization founded to preserve the memory of the deaths of the victims of the Holocaust, sought leave to intervene in the Crown's appeal against the acquittal of F on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity under
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code
. The moving party wished to intervene with respect to three issues: the constitutionality of ss. 7(3.71) and 7(3.74) of the Code, which was being attacked by F; the propriety of remarks made by defence counsel in his address to the jury; and whether the trial judge erred in his charge to the jury on the lack of medical evidence as to the cause of death during the train transports.
Held, the motion should be dismissed.
A criminal proceeding in which the accused is obliged to respond to submissions of more than one prosecutor lacks the appearance of fairness; that consideration was a sufficient reason for not granting leave to intervene on the issues relating to defence counsel's address and the charge to the jury. With respect to the constitutional issue, it did not appear that the assistance which the moving party could give to the court as an intervener would be different from that which would be given by the Attorney General of Canada.
MOTION for leave to intervene in a Crown appeal against the accused's acquittal on charges of having committed war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Rules respecting Criminal Proceedings, SI/85-152, Rule 28

Robert P. Armstrong, Q.C., and Linda Telgarsky, for Canadian
Holocaust Remembrance Association, moving party.
Thomas Lemon, for Attorney General of Canada, appellant.
Barbara Kulaszka, for respondent.

MORDEN A.C.J.O. (in Chambers):-- The Canadian Holocaust
Remembrance Association moves for an order under Rule 28 of the
Rules respecting Criminal Proceedings, SI/85-152, granting to
it leave to intervene in this appeal by the Attorney General of
Canada against the respondent's acquittal on an indictment
alleging that he committed certain "crimes against humanity"
and "war crimes".

These offences are defined and their prosecution is provided
for in
ss. 7(3.71)
to
7(3.77)
[all en. R.S.C. 1985, c. 30 (3rd
Supp.), s. 1(1)] in the
Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46
. On
the hearing of the appeal the respondent intends to submit that

ss. 7(3.71)
and 7(3.74) are void and of no effect because they
are inconsistent with several provisions (
ss. 7
,
11
(a) and (d),

12
and
15
are referred to) in the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
. He has served a notice of cross-appeal which sets
forth alternative grounds on which the acquittal should be
affirmed.

The moving party seeks leave to intervene with respect to
three issues: (1) the constitutionality of
ss. 7(3.71)
and

7(3.74)
of the
Criminal Code
; (2) the propriety of remarks made
by defence counsel in his address to the jury. The moving party
has submitted that its argument on this issue would be
restricted to ground number 9 in the appellant's notice of
appeal; (3) whether the trial judge erred in his charge to the
jury on the lack of medical evidence as to the cause of death
during the train transports. This does not relate expressly to
a ground of appeal as framed in the notice of appeal but it is
said to be "subsumed" under ground number 12 in the notice of
appeal. It reads:

12. That the learned trial judge erred in law in failing to
relate the relevant evidence to the different issues to be
determined by the jury and in particular in failing to
instruct them on inferences they could draw from various
facts and from circumstantial and documentary evidence.

The appellant and the respondent each oppose the granting of
leave to intervene.

Helen Smolack, the chairman of the moving party, deposes in
paras. 3 and 4 of her affidavit filed in support of the motion
as follows:

3. The CHRA is a non-profit organization found in 1978 to
foster and protect human rights by, in part, working to
ensure that an atrocity like the Holocaust never occurs
again.

4. The two major areas of concern perceived by the CHRA
since its inception have been:

(a)  preserving the memory of the deaths of millions of
people, primarily Jews, at the hands of Nazi Germany from
1933 to 1945 (the "Holocaust''), through public education and
through seeking the enforcement of Canadian and international
laws providing for the prosecution of Nazi war criminals
living in Canada; and

(b)  opposing the dissemination of all forms of hate
propaganda directed against Jews and seeking the enforcement
of Canadian laws which prohibit or restrict such practices.

Helen Smolack further deposes that "[s]ince its inception,
the CHRA has been actively engaged in making representations to
various levels of government and to judicial and quasi-judicial
bodies regarding the prohibition of hate propaganda and the
treatment of Nazi war criminals in Canada". Paragraphs 16 to 18
in her affidavit read:

16. The CHRA is concerned about the effective and fair
prosecution of war criminals pursuant to the provisions of
the
Criminal Code of Canada
dealing with the prosecution of
war criminals living in Canada. The CHRA is committed to
fighting and guarding against any possibility of a repeat of
the treatment of Jews in Europe in the 1930's and 1940's.

17. The CHRA views the prosecution of war criminals living
in Canada pursuant to the provisions of the
Criminal Code of
Canada
as a social and legal responsibility. The CHRA is
concerned about and interested in the use of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
to attack the relevant
provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada, to the detriment
of the fight against any possibility of a repeat of the
treatment of Jews in Europe in the 1930's and 1940's.

18. The CHRA views the requirement that war criminals be
prosecuted pursuant to the provisions of the
Criminal Code of
Canada
as fundamentally consistent with the principles of a
free and democratic society.

In R. v. Zundel
(1986), 16 O.A.C. 244 (C.A.)
, the League for
Human Rights of B'nai Brith Canada and the Canadian Jewish
Congress sought leave to intervene in an appeal from the
appellant's conviction of publishing a "statement or tale,
namely "Did Six Million Really Die?" that he knows is false and
that is likely to cause mischief to the public interest in
social and racial tolerance, contrary to (
s. 177
of) the

Criminal Code
". At p. 245 O.A.C. Howland C.J.O. said:

In R. v. Seaboyer and Gayme (1986),
1986 CanLII 7320 (ON CA)
, 50 C.R. (3d) 395, at p.
398, I pointed out that the right to intervene in criminal
proceedings, where the liberty of the subject is involved, is
one which should be granted sparingly. Here there are many
issues involved apart from the two issues on which
intervention is sought. It is very difficult to tell at this
juncture where a clear line of demarcation could be drawn.
While I am mindful of the deep interest and of the experience
of the applicants in their respective fields of hate
literature, racial discrimination and anti-semitism, I am not
persuaded that their special knowledge and expertise is so
closely linked with the matters in which they seek the right
of intervention as to justify the exercise of my discretion.
In reaching this conclusion I have borne in mind the fact
that the Crown will be responding to all of the issues which
have been raised by the appellant. In my opinion, in all the
circumstances, it does not require the assistance of the
applicants to illuminate any particular aspect of the appeal.

With respect to the first part of this passage, both fairness
and the appearance of fairness in the criminal law process are
of paramount concern. Under s. 7(3.75) of the
Criminal Code
the
prosecutor is the Attorney General of Canada or counsel acting
on his behalf. A criminal proceeding in which the accused
person is obliged to respond to submissions of more than one
prosecutor lacks the appearance of fairness. In my view, this
consideration is a sufficient reason for not granting leave to
intervene on the issues relating to defence counsel's address
and the trial judge's instructions to the jury. I note, also,
that what may be considered to be case-specific issues, such as
these, whose resolution is not likely to have ramifications
beyond the actual decision of the appeal, are not the kind of
issues on which leave to intervene is usually granted. One may
contrast, in this respect, other kinds of issues the decisions
on which affect not only the parties but also, potentially, the
state of the law.

A constitutional issue is clearly of the latter kind. It is
of particular importance that before deciding a constitutional
issue a court should know all the possibilities of choice open
to it as to the bases on which the issue can be decided. Only
with such knowledge can the court make the wisest decision.
Although the moving party has a profound interest in the
effective and fair prosecution of proceedings such as this one,
I am not persuaded, on the submissions made to me, that the
assistance which the moving party could give to the court as an
intervener would be different from that which will be given by
the Attorney General of Canada. In other words, it is not made
out in what way the moving party's different perspective
manifests itself in different submissions. The Attorney
General, of course, has an interest in defending the challenged
legislation on every basis that is relevant and possible and
has a corresponding duty of assisting the court.

I should note that in his submissions Mr. Armstrong placed
particular emphasis on the role that the moving party could
play in the justification of the challenged legislation under

s. 1
of the
Charter
. He submitted that the application of
s. 1

would be an issue that the court would have to consider. It
would appear that, if this is so, the relevant evidential or
factual considerations to which he referred relating to the
need for the legislation are ones which the Attorney General
would place before the court. If this necessarily involved the
assistance of the moving party, there is every reason to
believe that it would be forthcoming.

To the extent that precedent has a bearing on the making of a
discretionary decision, such as the one before me, I think that
this case is more like R. v. Zundel, supra, where intervention
was refused, than R. v. Seaboyer (1986),
1986 CanLII 7320 (ON CA)
, 50 C.R. (3d) 395 (Ont.
C.A.), referred to in Zundel, where leave to intervene was
granted.

For these reasons, the motion is dismissed.

Motion dismissed.
